title: Asa di Var close
hook: wonder, awe, sweetness, the thread of compassion

segments.voice: Yesterday, singing it at dawn, and your line: before sunrise. Did you give the first light to listening? Today we close the Asa di Var: four weeks of the dawn ballad, gathered like a pauri. Day five hundred sixty-three.

When the dawn singing ends, the sangat doesn't scatter right away. People stand for Ardas. Karah prashad, the warm sweet offering, is passed hand to hand. Someone folds the white sheets. Outside, the sun is fully up now, and the streets are filling with buses and school uniforms. Most people walk out carrying almost nothing: no notes, no book. Maybe one line, still humming in the back of the head. That's how the var has traveled for five centuries. Not mostly as a text people study, but as lines people carry out the door.
screen: `ARDAS, AND KARAH PRASHAD.` → `THE SUN FULLY UP.` → `ONE LINE CARRIED OUT THE DOOR.`

segments.voice: Let's walk the staircase once, from the top. The var: an old ballad of heroes, given new words and sung to a king's tune. The Guru who made angels out of men, a hundred times a day. A hundred moons, and still dark without the Guru. The One who made Himself and watches with delight. Then four steps of seeing: vismaad, wonder at every sound and color. Kudrat, power in seeing, eating, loving. Bhau, the wind and rivers moving in awe. And nirbhau, nirankar: only the Formless without fear. Then the people. The contented ones who served. Haumai, ego as a chronic illness, with its medicine inside it. Cartloads of books, and only one thing counted. Koorh, the false king and everything that passes. And sach: truth known only when the heart is true. Then the turnings. Pain the medicine, pleasure the disease. Mitthat neevee, sweetness and humility, the heavy side of the scale. The silk-cotton tree, tall and useless. And the sacrifice to the Guru, who put wisdom on the eyes. Then the thread. Compassion the cotton, contentment the thread, restraint the knot, truth the twist; a thread that won't break, burn, stain or be lost. Sootak moved inside: greed, lies, coveting, gossip. Fikka words that make a fikka life. The servant who argues. And finally the shape itself: pauris as steps, Guru Angad's second voice, and the whole thing sung as the sky turns gold. If there's one thread through all of it, it might be the one in the carry. The var keeps starting with wonder. Before it corrects anyone, it makes them look. Wonder first, then the work.
screen: `THE BALLAD, THE GURU, THE MOONS.` · `WONDER, POWER, AWE, THE FEARLESS.` · `EGO, KOORH, TRUTH, SWEETNESS.` · `THE THREAD, THE SERVANT, THE DAWN.` · then, large: `WONDER AT DAWN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: keep one salok. Sit and let the block pass through your mind once more: the wind in awe, the silk-cotton tree, the scale, the thread, dal without salt, the arguing servant. Don't try to hold them all. Wait for one to stay. Whichever one keeps coming back, that's yours. Say its picture to yourself in one sentence. Then breathe with it, the way the sangat carries a line out the door. If you pray, you can say Waheguru. The bell holds the time.
Asa di Var close. Twenty-four pauris and their saloks, sung at dawn: wonder, awe, truth, sweetness, and the thread of compassion.
Your line: wonder at dawn. Tomorrow morning, before anything else, look out a window for one full breath and let the first thing you feel be wonder. Day five hundred sixty-three.

howItsDone: Sikhs hear the Asa di Var sung in gurdwaras each morning, followed by Ardas and karah prashad, and many carry a favorite salok from it through the day.
